title: Data-visualisation best practice
examples: When should I use a pie chart instead of a bar graph?
What are the best practices for labeling axes on a graph?
How can I make my data visualization clearer for a non-expert audience?

explain.say: Today we are learning how to choose the right chart for your data.

draw.text: Chart Choice: When to use what

explain.say: If you want to show how something changes over many years, use a line chart.
To show how different parts make up a total amount, the pie chart is best.

draw.text: Pie Chart: Parts of a whole

explain.say: When comparing several unrelated items at one point in time, a bar chart works well.
Labeling is crucial; always title your graph clearly for the audience.
In a real report, if you show website traffic, use a line chart for the trend.

faq.q: Should I use a pie chart if the parts are very close in size?
faq.a: No, it becomes difficult for the audience to tell the difference accurately. Use a bar chart instead for better comparison.
asks: When is a pie chart misleading?
What if the percentages are similar?

faq.q: Does the chart type depend on the data source or the message?
faq.a: It depends more on the message you want to convey. The goal dictates the best visual representation for your data.
asks: What is the main purpose of choosing a chart?
Should I pick the chart that looks nicest?

faq.q: What should I label on the axes if my data is in percentages?

asks: How do I label percentage axes?
What units should I use for the axis?

faq.q: Is it okay to use multiple chart types in one presentation?
faq.a: It is generally best to stick to one or two consistent chart types to maintain clarity and focus for your audience.
asks: How many chart types are too many?

faq.q: When should I use a scatter plot versus a bar chart?
faq.a: Use a scatter plot when you are testing if two variables have a relationship, like height versus weight. Bar charts compare separate groups.
asks: When is a scatter plot better than bars?

facts: Bar charts are effective for comparing discrete categories.
Line charts are best for visualizing trends or changes over continuous intervals.
A pie chart should only represent parts that sum up to one hundred percent.
All charts require a clear title and labeled axes for proper interpretation.

quiz.say: You are tracking the global temperature increase over the last century. Which chart type is most appropriate?
quiz.why: A line chart clearly shows the continuous flow and rate of change over time.

wrong.0: A scatter plot shows relationships between two variables, not necessarily a single variable changing over time.
wrong.2: While bars show levels, they imply distinct, separate measurements rather than a continuous trend.
wrong.3: A pie chart suggests the parts make up a whole, which is not the case with temperature changes over time.

quiz.say: You need to show that a company's total revenue is split between three departments: Sales, Marketing, and R&D. What chart should you use?
quiz.why: Since the three departments must add up to the total revenue, a pie chart is the correct choice to show parts of a whole.

wrong.1: A bar chart would compare them as if they were separate totals, ignoring that they form one whole.
wrong.2: A line chart implies a progression or change over time, which is not the focus here.
wrong.3: This chart is designed to find relationships between two different measured variables.

quiz.say: If your graph shows 'Sales Volume' on the vertical axis and 'Month' on the horizontal axis, what must you label on the vertical axis?
quiz.why: The axis label tells the reader what the numbers actually represent, which is essential for correct interpretation.

wrong.0: The title describes the whole graph; the axis label describes the specific measurement on that line.
wrong.1: The year belongs on the horizontal axis if time is the independent variable.
wrong.2: The legend explains what different colored lines or bars mean, not what the numbers measure.
